analysis.one_liner: Lets companies pay independent contractors with stock while overriding state laws that treat gig workers as employees.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Patrick McHenry with six Republican cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let companies hand stock to independent contractors — including people who merely use their apps — under the same securities-registration exemption that applies to employee stock compensation, with the exemption's dollar cap rising with inflation each year. It would also wipe out any state law that presumes a gig worker is an employee for wage or benefit purposes, keeping those workers classified as contractors. The Government Accountability Office would study the effects three years after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits: App-based platform companies gain the most: they could keep workers classified as contractors even in states that tried to reclassify them, avoiding minimum wage, overtime, and benefit obligations under state law, while using stock grants as an alternative form of pay. Gig workers who prefer contractor flexibility and want a chance at equity upside also gain access to compensation that was previously reserved for employees.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the SEC's Rule 701 exemption — which lets companies issue securities as employee compensation without full registration — to independent contractors providing goods, labor, or services, and at the company's election to users of its platform.
Requires the SEC to raise the Rule 701 dollar cap annually with inflation, so the amount of stock a company can hand out grows each year.
Preempts any state law that creates a presumption that a gig worker is an employee for wage-rate or benefit purposes, keeping such workers outside state wage-and-hour and benefit mandates.
Requires a GAO study of the bill's effects, with a report to Congress within three years of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Gig workers who depend on state labor protections give them up: where a state presumes contractors are employees, this bill overrides that, so minimum wage, overtime, sick leave, and benefit rules would no longer reach them. State governments lose their authority over worker classification in this area. Workers receiving stock instead of part of their pay also bear the risk that those shares are worth little.

drawbacks.text: By preempting state employee-presumption laws for wages and benefits, the bill would strip gig workers of state minimum wage, overtime, and benefit protections in states that extended them, without creating any federal replacement.

Equity compensation is a risky substitute for wages: shares issued under this exemption are not registered with the SEC and typically carry resale restrictions, so they may be illiquid or end up worth far less than the pay they replace, and the bill provides no mechanism to value or guarantee them.
The bill's only evaluation of its effects is a GAO study due three years after enactment, meaning Congress would have made the state-law preemption permanent before learning how it played out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine upside — letting gig workers share in the equity of companies they work for — is narrow and risky, since unregistered shares may be worth little and workers could be paid in volatile stock instead of cash. The dominant provision is the state-law preemption, which removes wage and benefit protections from the very workers the bill's title invokes, and hands the classification fight to platform companies. On balance the costs to working contractors outweigh the equity opportunity, and the bill offers no federal floor to replace the state protections it nullifies.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Financial Services and Education and Labor committees the day it was introduced, and neither committee gave it a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Patrick McHenry introduced the bill on September 17, 2020, with Rep. Steve Stivers joining as the other original sponsor.
The same day, the House referred it to the Financial Services Committee and, in addition, to the Education and Labor Committee.
Six other House Republicans signed on as cosponsors; no Democrat did.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever recorded, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gig workers and the state governments that had moved to classify them as employees are better off, because the state wage and benefit protections the bill would have overridden remain in place. Platform companies did not get the federal shield they sought.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on, but the bill never reached a vote, so no one's position was ever recorded on the floor.

industries.note: The bill keeps their workers classified as contractors even in states with employee-presumption laws, freeing platforms from state minimum wage, overtime, and benefit obligations, while letting them substitute unregistered stock for pay. The cost of that flexibility falls on the workers themselves, whose legal protections would be voided.

Any state law presuming gig workers are employees for wage or benefit purposes would be preempted, taking classification authority away from states that had used it to extend protections to gig workers.

industries.industry: Securities lawyers and equity-compensation service providers
industries.note: Extending Rule 701 to contractors and indexing its cap to inflation would expand the market for designing and administering stock-based compensation for non-employees.
